doc.title: Slide Hampton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Practice, Indianapolis memories and the trombone
title: Family bands and Oscar Pettiford
summary: Hampton learned about other family bands later and praises Pettiford's role in bass literature.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: When you were in the Hampton family band days, in articles you mentioned the Pettiford family, and I just made a joke the other day about the Marsalis thing – how aware were you of other family bands, and of the tradition of family bands? Or did you just take it for granted, because that’s what your family did?

No, actually I became more aware of it later. When we were in the family band, we didn’t – we were in Indianapolis. So we didn’t have a lot of the news that was available to us. I learned later, after meeting Jimmy, and also, I didn’t meet him, but I heard Oscar Pettiford and several of the family bands, the older families.

Yeah. Oscar Pettiford was one of the very important people himself that must have either come from an influence of his family, or he influenced them, because he’s the guy that really started showing the bass players that there was a new literature going to start developing for the bass. It started with Oscar Pettiford and Jimmy Blanton, a new literature, which – by this time, the bass has developed a literature that’s incredible, but that started with Oscar Pettiford, and the classical players, because all the good bass players studied classically. The bass, of course, was in existence long before this country was even in existence, I mean, as America. The bass was in existence in Europe for a long time before that.
